Orthopaedic Trauma Reference · Region 06 · Pelvis

Pelvic Ring Injuries

Mechanism-based classification, resuscitation, and stabilization of the pelvis as a ring structure — from APC I to triangular osteosynthesis.

R&G CHAPTER 50 AO/OTA 61 YOUNG & BURGESS · TILE · DENIS ANTERIOR & POSTERIOR FIXATION

Overview

The pelvis is a ring structure. A single break may be stable; unstable injuries always involve at least two areas. Stability — not just radiographic appearance — drives treatment. Hemodynamic instability often parallels mechanical instability.

Incidence
0.82 per 100,000 (overall mean age 45; 18–44 yr peak; geriatric 22%; M:F 56:44).
Mortality
Hemodynamically stable on presentation: 3%. Hypotensive on presentation: 32–38%.
Mechanism (Young)
APC, LC, VS, CM. APC overall mortality 2–3× higher than LC injuries.
Associated injuries
Chest 63% · Long bone 50% · Head 40% · Solid organ 40% · Spine 25% · GI 14%.
Genitourinary
Bladder/urethra in 6–15%. Male urethral injury more common; female vagina protected (0–5%). Bladder rupture: 60% EPBR · 30% IPBR · 10% both.
Open pelvic injuries
~5% of pelvic fractures. Jones class 3 (rectal/perineal wound + unstable) → up to 44–50% mortality.

Initial Resuscitation Priorities

  • Identify and tamponade bleeding: ATLS protocol, massive transfusion if needed. Most pelvic deaths from arterial/venous disruption.
  • Close the ring early: Sheet or commercial binder at greater trochanter level reduces pelvic volume for tamponade. ~180 N force closes APC ring in cadaveric model.
  • Internal rotation of lower extremities: Assists reduction of open-book injuries; adduction adds compression.
  • Hematoma >500 cm³ on CT carries 4.8× increased risk of arterial injury / need for angiography.
  • Contrast extravasation on CT: EAST Level 1 recommendation for angiography regardless of hemodynamic status.

Imaging Workflow

  • AP pelvis — initial trauma series; assess symphysis, SI joints, sacral foramina, iliac wings, rami.
  • Inlet view — beam directed caudally (ideal ~25°); evaluates AP translation, posterior pelvic ring, sacral promontory profile.
  • Outlet view — beam directed cephalad (ideal ~60°); evaluates vertical displacement, sacral foramina.
  • CT with 1–2 mm cuts + 3D reconstructions: identifies subtle injuries; defines safe corridors for IS screws; sagittal reconstructions detect kyphosis (U-shaped sacral fracture, spinopelvic dissociation).
  • Fluoroscopic stress (EUA) — Sagi popularized; >10 mm overlap of rami on stress = positive for instability. 41% of presumed-stable patterns proved unstable on stress in original series.

Hemorrhage Control Ladder

InterventionIndication / Notes
Pelvic binder / sheetFirst-line for APC. Apply at greater trochanters. Theoretical concern with LC overreduction. Remove within 24 h if stable.
External fixatorIliac crest or supra-acetabular pins. Useful when binder fails or for laparotomy access.
Angiography & embolizationMandatory if contrast extravasation on CT. <60 min from arrival significantly reduces mortality. Selective > nonselective (less thromboembolic complications).
Preperitoneal pelvic packingDamage-control adjunct (EAST Level 3). Requires stabilized ring (binder/ex-fix/C-clamp) as wall against packing. Higher VTE risk vs. AE.
REBOATemporizing for shock as alternative to resuscitative thoracotomy. Complications include amputation, hematoma, pseudoaneurysm.

Tile/AO ↔ Young-Burgess equivalence
APC I ≈ Tile B-rotational stable · APC II ≈ Tile B1 · APC III & VS ≈ Tile C · LC I ≈ Tile B-rotational stable (mostly) · LC II/III ≈ Tile B2/B3.

Anatomy & Biomechanics

The pelvis = sacrum + 2 innominate bones (each ilium + ischium + pubis fused at triradiate). The posterior ring provides ~85% of stability; the symphysis only ~15%.

Osseous Anatomy

  • Innominate bone: ilium, ischium, pubis — fuse at triradiate cartilage where acetabulum develops.
  • Iliac columns: anterior column (ischial tuberosity → SI joint) for sitting load; posterior column (acetabular dome → SI joint) for standing load. The sciatic buttress spans both — densest bone in pelvis (target for supra-acetabular pins / IS screw cortical purchase).
  • Sacrum: 5 fused vertebral bodies. Posterior convex / anterior concave with variable kyphosis. Sacral dysmorphism in ~41% — lumbarization of S1 or sacralization of L5, unilateral or bilateral; alters safe corridors for IS screws.
  • Spinopelvic junction: sacrum articulates with L5 via L5–S1 disc and facets; force transfer from spine through sacrum → SI joints → ilium → acetabulum → lower extremities.

Ligamentous Anatomy — Stability Domino

  • Posterior SI complex (interosseous, short posterior, long posterior SI ligaments): the strongest ligaments in the body; primary stabilizers of the posterior ring.
  • Anterior sacroiliac ligaments (ASI): weaker; fail before PSILs in external rotation. Average failure at 2.2 cm symphysis diastasis in cadaveric model (cutoff classically >2.5 cm).
  • Sacrotuberous (ST) + sacrospinous (SSp) ligaments: resist external rotation and vertical shear of hemipelvis. Originate from sacrum and coccyx, insert on ischial tuberosity (ST) and ischial spine (SSp).
  • Iliolumbar ligament (ILL): L4/L5 transverse process to iliac crest. L5 transverse process avulsion = pelvic instability marker (though only 19% sensitivity for vertical instability per Mendel).
  • Symphyseal ligaments: superior and arcuate (inferior). Account for only 15% of pelvic ring stability.

Ligament Failure Sequence (APC Mechanism)

Force ProgressionStructures FailingResulting Pattern
Initial external rotationSymphyseal ligaments (anterior arcuate)APC I — <2.5 cm diastasis
Continued external rotationST → SSp → ASI ligaments (sequentially)APC II — >2.5 cm; PSILs intact (posterior hinge)
Maximum external rotationIntra-articular + posterior SI ligamentsAPC III — complete instability, pelvic floor disrupted

Critical Neurovascular Relationships

  • L5 nerve root: courses on anterior sacral ala ~1 cm medial to SI joint at pelvic brim. Closest at most anterior aspect of SI joint — keep dissection posterior or at sacral promontory. At highest risk during sacral fracture reduction and IS screw placement (anterior cortex breach).
  • S1 nerve root tunnel: caudal/posterior to iliac cortical density (ICD) on lateral view; central → anterolateral on inlet; "hip-spica" pattern on outlet. IS screw must stay anterior in S1 body, beneath ICD.
  • Internal iliac artery and branches: lie anterior to SI joint. Superior gluteal artery exits greater sciatic notch — most common bleeding source. Other commonly injured branches: lateral sacral, internal pudendal, inferior gluteal, obturator.
  • Corona mortis: anastomosis between obturator artery and external iliac artery (or its branches) — averages ~6 cm from symphysis on inside of superior pubic ramus. Catastrophic bleeding if violated during Stoppa exposure or retrograde rami screw.
  • Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (LFCN): exits pelvis under inguinal ligament near ASIS — at risk during anterior approach, supra-acetabular pin placement, and INFIX (25% irritation rate).
  • Bladder and urethra: immediately posterior to symphysis. Distended bladder ruptures with compression; male urethra (long, anterior + posterior portions) more vulnerable than female (short, protected by vagina).

Biomechanics

  • Bilateral stance: symphysis and inferior SI joint under tension; superior SI under compression.
  • Single-leg stance: symphysis under compression and vertical shear; superior SI under tension, inferior SI under compression.
  • If symphysis disrupted but posterior ligaments intact (APC I) → compression prevails → diastasis closes with mobilization (rationale for nonoperative management).
  • If ASI ligaments ALSO disrupted (APC II) → tension at symphysis persists with weight bearing → surgical intervention warranted.
  • External fixation and internal fixation are biomechanically equivalent for external rotation control, but internal fixation is superior for resisting vertical displacement.

Classification

Three commonly cited systems. Young-Burgess (mechanism) is the most widely used and predicts associated injuries. Tile/AO-OTA (stability) guides surgical decisions. Denis classifies sacral fractures and predicts neurologic risk.

AO/OTA Pelvic Ring Subgroups (61-A / B / C)

Sacral Classifications

SystemKey Features
Denis Zone ILateral to foramina (~50%). Low neurologic injury rate.
Denis Zone IITransforaminal (~⅓). ~30% neurologic deficit (L5, S1, S2 roots).
Denis Zone IIIMedial to foramina / spinal canal (~16%). Up to 60% neurologic injury. U/H/T/Y patterns = spinopelvic dissociation.
Roy-Camille (modified)Type I: kyphosis without translation · Type II: kyphosis + posterior translation · Type III: complete translation (cephalad fragment anterior) · Type IV: comminution without displacement.
AOSpine sacralMorphology (A/B/C) + neurology + modifiers. Type C1 = vertical fracture with L5/S1 facet involvement (spinopelvic implications).

Fragility Fractures of the Pelvis (Rommens & Hoffmann — FFP)

  • FFP I: anterior ring only (Ia unilateral; Ib bilateral) — nonoperative.
  • FFP II: nondisplaced posterior injury ± anterior involvement (IIa–c) — operative considered.
  • FFP III: displaced unilateral posterior injury (IIIa–c) — surgical recommended.
  • FFP IV: bilateral posterior involvement (IVa–c) — surgical with multidisciplinary input.

ClassDescriptionRisk
1Open injury, stable pelvic ringLowest

3Rotationally/vertically unstable, rectal/perineal wound with fecal contamination44% sepsis-related mortality
Interobserver Reliability
Both Tile/AO and Young-Burgess have low interobserver reliability — yet both predict mortality, transfusion, and associated injury. Use classifications as decision aids, not as ends.

Management

Two parallel goals: hemodynamic stabilization and mechanical stabilization. The posterior ring is the more critical stabilizer — anterior fixation alone cannot restore stability with complete posterior disruption.

Nonoperative — Indications

  • Stable pelvic ring injuries: APC I, many LC I, FFP I.
  • Stable/incomplete sacral fractures.
  • Patients too sick to undergo surgery.
  • Low-energy osteoporotic pelvic injuries when ambulating with ADLs.

LC I controversy: Beckmann survey of OTA members showed only 33% agreement on treatment. If complete sacral fracture (Denis II) present, agreement on surgical stabilization rises. Comminuted rami fractures predict displacement; absence of inferior rami fracture predicted 100% nondisplacement in one series. EUA in OR or fluoroscopic stress (Sagi/Parry/DeKeyser) can identify occult instability.

Nonoperative Protocol

  • APC I: weight bearing as tolerated. Internal rotation of bilateral LE for comfort. Repeat AP at 1–2 weeks post-mobilization.
  • LC I: historically TDWB 6–12 weeks → now WBAT as pain allows. Repeat imaging after ambulation; further x-rays only if symptomatic.
  • FFP I osteoporotic: PTH 1–84 (100 µg daily) significantly improves pain, VAS, "up-and-go" test, and union rate (100% vs 9% in RCT).

Operative Indications — Anterior Ring

  • Symphyseal dislocations with >2.5 cm diastasis on static or dynamic (EUA) imaging.
  • Augmentation of posterior fixation in vertically displaced or completely unstable injuries.
  • Augmentation of poor posterior fixation in osteopenic bone.
  • Significantly displaced rami fractures, locked symphysis, straddle fractures (bilateral superior + inferior rami).
  • Pain and inability to mobilize (relative).

Operative Indications — Posterior Ring

  • Complete disruption of SI joint with anterior + posterior SI ligaments.
  • Any posterior ring injury with vertical displacement or propensity.
  • Displaced crescent fractures (iliac wing fractures entering crest and exiting greater sciatic notch or SI joint).
  • Complete sacral fractures with displacement potential.
  • Lumbopelvic dissociation.
  • Augmentation of anterior fixation in APC II.

Fixation Strategies — Anterior Ring

ConstructBest UseNotes
Symphyseal plate (precontoured small fragment)Symphysis diastasis >2.5 cm (APC II/III)3 × 3.5-mm screws/side preferred. Six-hole curved recon has higher failure than precontoured.
Anterior external fixator (iliac crest or AIIS/supra-acetabular)Emergent stabilization, contaminated soft tissue, SPT, bilateral ramiSupra-acetabular pins biomechanically superior. Author preferred over iliac crest.
INFIX (pedicle screws + subcutaneous rod)Obese patient, soft-tissue contraindication to ORIFLFCN irritation 25%, HO 25%, infection 3%. Keep screw heads ≥1.5 cm above AIIS.

Antegrade superior ramus screwLateral or pubic root rami, obese patientsStart posteroinferior to ASIS. Obturator-outlet (teepee) + inlet views.

ConstructBest UseNotes
Iliosacral (IS) screw (S1 ± S2)SI joint disruption, sacral fracture with anatomic reductionLag with washer for compression. Fully threaded if comminuted to avoid nerve injury.
Transsacral / transiliac-transsacral screwBilateral injuries, vertical instability, augmentationDefault to S2 in dysmorphic sacrum.
Posterior tension band plate / sacral barsAdjunct or alternative when corridors too narrowOpen posterior approach required.

Operative Principles

  • Posterior first ideally — posterior reduction restores ring stability; anterior alone cannot maintain reduction if posterior unstable.
  • Alternatively, reducing widely displaced anterior ring can aid posterior reduction — keep anterior fixation "flexible" while reducing posterior.
  • Avoid orthogonal plating — overly stiff anterior construct prevents posterior manipulation, especially with anterior malreduction.
  • External fixator across the SI joint for APC requires two points of fixation to provide rotational stability.
  • In osteoporotic bone, consider cement-augmented IS screws or larger-caliber (porous coated) implants for "rescue" purchase.
  • VS sacral fracture: longitudinal traction first, then medial translation. AP iliac crests, acetabular domes, ischial tuberosities should align bilaterally before fixation.
Reduction Quality Matters
Kellam: with adequate reduction (<2 cm symphysis), 100% returned to normal function in rotationally unstable injuries. With associated posterior pathology, only 31% reached normal function. Anatomic reduction of posterior ring → improved Majeed/SF-36 scores at long-term follow-up.

Surgical Approaches

Anterior approaches (Pfannenstiel, Stoppa, lateral window of ilioinguinal) for symphysis, rami, SI joint, iliac wing. Posterior approaches (paramedian Wiltse or midline) for sacral fractures and posterior SI joint. Percutaneous techniques (IS screw, rami screw) dominate modern practice.

Anterior Approach to SI Joint (Lateral Window of Ilioinguinal)

  • Skin incision 1–2 cm posterior to ASIS along iliac crest (avoid LFCN). 5–6 cm typical length.
  • External oblique taken off crest with 1–2 cm cuff for closure.
  • Subperiosteal iliacus elevation from inner table — bone wax for bleeding from nutrient foramen (typically just distal/lateral to anterior SI joint).
  • Psoas elevated over pelvic brim — malleable or radiolucent retractor protects abdominal/pelvic contents.
  • L5 nerve root palpated on anterior ala — push gently with Kittner during medial dissection.
  • Allows direct visualization of anterior SI joint and reduction with Schanz pin in PSIS as joystick + two clamps (cranial + caudal).

Posterior Approach for Sacral Fractures & SI Joint

  • Prone on radiolucent Jackson table. Confirm no chest support shadowing fluoro. Distal femoral traction pin if needed.
  • Prone positioning corrects ~10° of sacral kyphosis. Additional bumps under chest/thighs for more correction.
  • Paramedian incision just medial to PSIS for SI joint or unilateral sacral; midline incision (L4 spinous process to anus) for bilateral sacral fractures or transverse components.
  • Multifidus elevated from spinous processes; preserve PSILs which remain intact in sacral fractures.
  • For decompression: lamina spreader gently into fracture, irrigate clot, identify and protect nerve root; pituitary rongeur for partial laminectomy if needed.
  • Beware occult spina bifida (up to 15%) — avoid blind midline dissection into spinal canal.

ORIF Iliac Wing & Crescent Fractures

  • Either anterior (lateral window) or posterior approach depending on fracture location (Tornetta cadaveric: >2.5 cm lateral to ILL footprint → anterior; medial → posterior).
  • Modified straight-straight Weber clamp for transverse iliac fractures; ball spike pusher for translation reduction.
  • Fixation at pelvic brim and along crest — central wing is thin (avoid hardware here). Lag screws along crest provide fixation + compression.
  • Open fractures: minimize surface implants; use crest-to-brim or crest-to-posterior-column screws.

Stoppa (Modified) Approach

  • Extends Pfannenstiel through midline rectus split.
  • Hip flexion + knee bump relaxes neurovascular bundle for retraction.
  • Identify and ligate corona mortis (~6 cm from symphysis on inside of superior ramus) before further dissection.
  • Allows access to medial superior ramus, quadrilateral surface, pelvic brim — useful for high rami fractures or associated acetabular injuries.

Complications

Intraoperative Hemorrhage

  • Corona mortis: most catastrophic intraoperative bleed during anterior approaches. Pack, identify, ligate. If uncontrolled — close skin and emergent angio-embolization.
  • Superior gluteal artery: at risk near greater sciatic notch during posterior dissection — embolization preferred over ligation (recurrent collaterals).
  • External iliac vessels: at risk during Stoppa and over-laterally placed retropubic drains.

Inability to Achieve Adequate Fixation / Poor Bone

  • Cement augmentation of IS screws (calcium phosphate) — increases stiffness and pullout strength.
  • Larger-caliber porous-coated screws (8–11.5 mm) for "rescue" in dysmorphic or osteoporotic bone.
  • Crossed symphysis screws for poor pubic body purchase.
  • Locked symphysis plate only when bone is extremely poor (no biomechanical advantage in normal bone, can fail catastrophically).

Loss of Fixation & Reduction

  • Premature weight bearing and underappreciated posterior instability are leading causes of symphysis plate failure.
  • In APC II series, anterior-only fixation had significantly higher plate failure and malunion vs combined anterior + posterior fixation.
  • Two-hole symphysis plates have high failure rate — avoid. Use 4–6 hole precontoured symphyseal-specific plates.
  • Hardware failure is common but does not correlate with functional outcome — implant removal not routinely warranted for asymptomatic failure.

Infection

  • Pin tract infection: common with external fixation, especially in obese (large pannus). Daily pin care; superficial → oral antibiotics; deep purulence → debridement.
  • Wound dehiscence: Pfannenstiel and posterior midline incisions; obese patients at highest risk. Drainage of space of Retzius and subcutaneous layer.
  • Hardware infection from urinary contamination: SPT placement should be FAR from anterior approach incisions. EPBR repair can be done at same setting as ORIF anterior; severe contamination → use ex-fix instead of internal hardware.
  • INFIX infection rate ~3% in systematic review.

Thromboembolism

  • High-risk population — chemical prophylaxis (LMWH) typically started 24–48 h after fixation if no contraindication.
  • Pelvic packing carries 9.8% greater absolute VTE risk vs angio-embolization in one large database study.
  • IVC filter for prolonged immobilization with absolute contraindication to anticoagulation.
  • Duration: minimum 6 weeks; longer based on mobility and associated injuries.

Heterotopic Ossification

  • INFIX: HO around supra-acetabular pins in 24–50% of patients — usually asymptomatic; correlates with age and ISS.
  • Symptomatic HO can be debrided at time of implant removal.
  • Routine prophylaxis (indomethacin/radiation) not standard for pelvic ring fixation.

Symptomatic Hardware

  • Symphysis plates: implant failure is common but rarely symptomatic — removal not routinely indicated. Female childbearing considerations are obstetrician-dependent; vaginal delivery successful with retained hardware in published series.
  • Prominent IS screw heads — washer minimizes intrusion and erosion of iliac cortex.
  • Retrograde rami screws can be prominent at medial entry point near pubic tubercle — appropriate length and cannulated countersinking.

Functional Outcomes

  • Even with anatomic reduction and both anterior + posterior fixation: SF-36 physical score ~20% below population norms at 1 year; physical function ~69% of normal.
  • Posterior ring involvement (P or A/P groups) → significantly worse long-term outcome than isolated anterior (A) injury.
  • Sexual dysfunction: 25% of patients report significant sexual problems at long-term follow-up (no Tile A/B/C difference).
  • Outcomes scores (Majeed, Iowa Pelvic Score, Orlando, Hannover) have limited responsiveness/validation — heterogeneous patient populations confound interpretation.
  • Recovery trajectory: SF-36 PCS improves between 6–12 months and 1–5 years for surgically treated 61-B/C injuries, but does NOT return to baseline at 5 years.
Long-term Recovery Reality
Counsel patients with unstable pelvic ring injuries that even with successful reduction and union, full functional recovery may take years and may remain incomplete. Long-term sexual, bowel, and bladder dysfunction is common — especially with Denis zone II/III sacral injury.
